title: At the end of life
hook: Pure Land practice at the deathbed: the name said with the dying

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chan and Pure Land together: silent sitting in the morning, the name in the afternoon, a tiger with horns. Your line was both together. Did you pair a still minute with one word? Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

A hospital room, late at night. The machines have been turned down. An old woman lies still, her breathing slow and shallow. Around the bed, her family and a few friends from the temple stand close, and they are chanting, softly, steadily: Amituofo, Amituofo. When one voice tires, another picks it up. She may not be able to speak anymore. She may not even be able to open her eyes. But the name keeps going, just above her, like a handrail she can reach for in the dark. Today: at the end of life.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `FAMILY CHANTING SOFTLY.` → `THE NAME LIKE A HANDRAIL.`

segments.voice: First, the root. We met it a week ago: in the Contemplation Sutra, a dying man too pressed by pain to picture anything, and a good friend at his side who tells him to just say the name. Some Pure Land teachers trace deathbed practice to that friend. The point isn't only what the dying person can do. It's who is sitting with them. Second, in China. The practice of chanting the name with and for the dying has its own name, zhunian, helping recitation. People take turns, so the name never stops, and the dying person can follow it with their mind even when they no longer have the breath to say it. Third, in Japan. Tradition says the monk Genshin, in his book on birth in the Pure Land, described deathbed rites: an image of Amida set facing west, and colored threads tied from the image's hand to the hand of the dying, a thread to hold on the way. Fourth, where teachers differ. For Shinran, birth in the Pure Land is settled in this life, the moment shinjin is given. So in Shin Buddhism the last hour is not a test, and there's no need to wait anxiously for Amida to come at death. Other Pure Land communities place great weight on the deathbed and the last thought of the name. Both, in their own ways, do the same simple thing for the person in the bed: they don't leave them alone with the dark. They keep the name going.
screen: `A GOOD FRIEND AT THE BEDSIDE.` · `HELPING RECITATION: TAKING TURNS.` · `THREADS FROM AMIDA'S HAND.` · `SETTLED IN LIFE, OR AT THE LAST BREATH.` · then, large: `THE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone in the light. Settle, and breathe gently. Bring to mind someone who is ill, or old, or near the end, or someone who has already died. If no one comes, hold the idea of a stranger in a hospital bed tonight. Picture them resting in a soft, wide light, the way Pure Land Buddhists picture the light of Amitabha. If you say the name, you can say it for them, quietly. If not, just keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
At the end of life. Pure Land practice at the deathbed: the name said with the dying, so no one meets the dark alone. Today's word.
screen: `AT THE END OF LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the name at the end. Today, think of someone who is caring for a person who is ill or old, and offer to take one turn, the way voices take turns at the bedside: an errand, a meal, an hour, so they can rest. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In Chinese Pure Land communities, family and temple members take turns chanting Amitabha's name at the bedside of the dying; Japanese Pure Land traditions have their own deathbed rites, and in Shin Buddhism, where birth is understood as settled in life, the nembutsu is said at the end in gratitude.
